title: How badly can column-pivoted QR choose rows of an orthonormal basis? The sharp stretched-exponential worst case
shortTitle: The sharp worst case of column-pivoted QR on orthonormal rows
oneLine: Greedy row selection loses at most exp(C(H)√k) against the best possible, with an exact constant, not 2^k.
abstract: Many numerical methods keep k of the N coordinates of an N×k matrix Q with orthonormal columns, for example the interpolation points of the discrete empirical interpolation method (DEIM). The quality of a choice I is γ = ‖Q(I,:)⁻¹‖₂, the factor by which interpolation from the chosen coordinates can be worse than the best approximation; some choice always has γ ≤ √(k(N−k+1)). The rule used in practice is column-pivoted QR (QRCP) on Q*, whose classical guarantee (Drmač and Gugercin) grows like 2ᵏ. Chen, Liu, He and Dong gave the first answer to Problem 4.3 of Amsel et al.: QRCP can be worse than every polynomial multiple of the existence scale, and their construction already gives growth of order exp(c√k). This candidate determines the worst case on the logarithmic scale. If the coherence μ(Q), the largest row energy divided by the average, is at most H, every legal QRCP selection satisfies γ ≤ √(e(N−k+1)) exp(C(H)√k) with an explicit constant C(H): C(1) = 2 and C(2) ≈ 2.25. Matching examples show that C(H) cannot be lowered (at H = 1 under the smallest-label tie rule). Since μ(Q) ≤ N/k, the bound needs no assumption; without one, the worst case is exp(Θ(√(k log(N/k)))) once N ≥ k^(2+ε). An a posteriori bound from the observed pivots has an optimal coefficient. Limits: exact arithmetic and worst cases only; sharpness is on the logarithmic scale, with a factor polynomial in k remaining; the worst examples need N of order k³, and the regime N = O(k) is open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 2.3 (proof): if the coherence is at most H, every legal QRCP selection, with any tie-breaking, satisfies γ ≤ √(e(N−k+1)) exp(C(H)√k), where C(H) = √ρ + 1/√ρ and ρ − log ρ = 1 + log H; C(1) = 2, C(2) ≈ 2.25 and C(H)²/log H → 1.

Theorem 2.3 (proof): the constant is sharp on the logarithmic scale, log G_k(H) = (C(H) + o(1))√k, with real examples of fewer than 3k³ rows and unique pivots for H > 1, and with the smallest-label tie rule at H = 1.
Corollary 2.6 (proof): every orthonormal input satisfies γ ≤ √(e(N−k+1)) exp(C(N/k)√k), so no coherence assumption is needed.
Theorem 2.7 and Corollary 2.8 (proof): without any assumption the worst case is exp(Θ(√(k log(N/k)))) once N ≥ k^(2+ε) and log N = o(k), and exp((1+o(1))√(k log N)) when log N/log k → ∞.
Theorem 7.1 and Proposition 7.2 (proof): γ ≤ (√e/d_k) exp(√((k−1)L)) from the observed pivot range L = log(d₁²/d_k²), with an optimal coefficient.
Table 2 (computation): the new bound is smaller than the classical one from k = 13 at H = 1; at k = 100 it allows about 10⁹ to 10¹⁰ where the classical bound allowed about 10³⁰.

narration:
This is an audio briefing from Evidence Press on a research candidate about how a standard computer routine chooses measurement points.

Many simulations keep only a few measurement points out of thousands. You have a handful of important patterns, say the main modes of a fluid flow, and you want to read just a few values and still reconstruct the rest. The usual way to pick the points is a greedy rule built into every linear algebra library, called column-pivoted QR: again and again, take the point that the points already chosen explain least.

One number measures the choice: the factor by which reconstruction from the chosen points can be worse than the best possible. Good choices always exist. The textbook guarantee for the greedy rule, from Drmač and Gugercin, only said that this factor grows exponentially. A workshop list of open problems asked whether the greedy rule does nearly as well as the best choices. Chen, Liu, He and Dong answered first: no, and their examples already grow like the exponential of a small multiple of the square root of the number of patterns.

This paper finds the exact worst case. The greedy rule is never worse than the exponential of a constant times that square root, and the constant is exact. It is two when every point carries the same share of energy, and it grows slowly as the energy becomes less even. For a hundred patterns, the old guarantee is a number with thirty digits; the new one has only nine or ten digits. Examples come as close to the bound as you like, so the constant cannot be lowered, and the bound needs no assumption at all.

The idea is that the greedy rule controls every chosen column on every block of trailing coordinates at once. A carefully shaped rescaling turns this into a bound on a triangular matrix, and a determinant argument finishes the job. The matching examples hide a classical triangular matrix, due to Kahan, inside a much larger one.

The limits matter. The results are about exact arithmetic and worst cases; typical inputs behave far better. Sharp means the leading term of the exponent, and the worst examples need very many points compared with patterns. The practical advice: measure the factor after choosing the points, which is cheap, and switch to a safer rule if it is large.

This is an unrefereed candidate. Its checking is internal AI-assisted review and computation, not peer review. This briefing uses a synthetic voice and is not additional evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Chen, Liu, He and Dong (2026), Iteris: Agentic Research Loops for Computational Mathematics. arXiv preprint. Gives the first, negative answer to Problem 4.3 of Amsel et al.; the construction in its Appendix B (Lemma 24) already gives growth of order exp(c√k) for every c below ½√(log H).

Amsel et al. (2026), Linear Systems and Eigenvalue Problems: Open Questions from a Simons Workshop. arXiv preprint (versions 1 and 3). Problem 4.3, posed by Damle and Kressner, asks whether column-pivoted QR meets the existence scale on orthonormal rows; version 3 records the answers.

Drmač and Gugercin (2016), A New Selection Operator for the Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method — Improved A Priori Error Bound and Extensions. SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing. Theorem 2.1 is the classical bound that grows like 2^k.
Damle (2026), Computing Strong Rank-Revealing Factorizations for Matrices with Orthonormal Rows. arXiv preprint. Shows that Bischof–Stewart pivoting meets the existence scale on orthonormal rows.

Engler (1997), The behavior of the QR-factorization algorithm with column pivoting. Applied Mathematics Letters. The pivot floor used in Lemma 3.1, the average-determinant property and Hadamard completions.
Kahan (1966), Numerical Linear Algebra. Canadian Mathematical Bulletin. The classical triangular matrix behind the matching examples.
Sra (2026, as "Count ex Machina"), GPT, the Counterexample Machine. arXiv preprint. Records a small exact example with k = 3 and N = 8 (Appendix A.5).

Gu and Eisenstat (1996), Efficient Algorithms for Computing a Strong Rank-Revealing QR Factorization. SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing. Strong rank-revealing QR, a selection rule with a polynomial guarantee.
Drmač and Veselić (2008), New Fast and Accurate Jacobi SVD Algorithm. I. SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications. Related work on scaled triangular inverses (a different quantity).
Gilles (2026), Convergence rates for pivoted QR and LU. arXiv preprint. Approximation error of pivoted QR under singular-value decay (a different quantity).
Rusu and Dobra (2007), Pseudo-random number generation for sketch-based estimations. ACM Transactions on Database Systems. The finite-field sign construction used in Appendix A.
